clinicalPearls: Typically affects young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance, and often in patients who are myopic
Presents with acute onset of photopsia (shimmering or flickering lights) and one or more zones of visual field loss, frequently in the peripapillary region
The fundus characteristically looks normal or near-normal early in the disease, so the retinopathy is described as occult
Electroretinography is key to diagnosis, revealing outer retinal dysfunction in affected zones despite an unremarkable fundus appearance
Fundus autofluorescence commonly shows a demarcating line or trizonal pattern separating normal from affected retina and is very useful for detecting and monitoring lesions
Optical coherence tomography demonstrates disruption or loss of the outer retinal bands (ellipsoid zone) corresponding to the symptomatic field defect
Over time affected zones may develop pigmentary changes and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, and disease can be unilateral or bilateral
Management is debated and there is no proven therapy; observation is common and immunosuppression is sometimes used in progressive cases
reference.pathophysiology: Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy is characterised by dysfunction and degeneration of the photoreceptors and outer retina in discrete zones, often beginning adjacent to the optic disc and spreading. The precise mechanism is uncertain, but an autoimmune or inflammatory process targeting photoreceptors, possibly triggered in genetically susceptible individuals, is favoured; a viral prodrome is sometimes reported. Loss of the ellipsoid zone and photoreceptor outer segments produces the field defects and photopsias, while the retinal pigment epithelium and inner retina are relatively preserved early, explaining the near-normal fundus and the value of functional and autofluorescence imaging. Chronic disease leads to zonal outer retinal atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Multifocal choroiditis and other white dot syndromes
Retinitis pigmentosa and other inherited photoreceptor dystrophies
Optic neuritis or other optic neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Full-field and multifocal electroretinography to demonstrate zonal outer retinal dysfunction
Fundus autofluorescence to identify demarcation lines and the trizonal pattern
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography to show ellipsoid zone disruption
Automated visual field testing to map and monitor the scotoma and often an enlarged blind spot
Fluorescein angiography, usually unremarkable, to exclude inflammatory or vascular mimics
Investigation for paraneoplastic retinopathy and antiretinal antibodies when clinically suspected
redFlags: Progressive enlargement of field loss threatening central vision
Bilateral or rapidly advancing disease suggesting a more aggressive process
Features raising concern for paraneoplastic retinopathy and underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many patients stabilise with persistent but non-progressive field defects and reasonable central acuity, though photopsias and scotomata may remain; a minority experience progressive or recurrent disease with expanding zones of atrophy and permanent visual field loss.
pitfalls: Dismissing a patient with photopsia and field loss as functional because the fundus looks normal
Failing to obtain electroretinography and autofluorescence, which reveal the occult pathology
Missing an underlying malignancy in what is actually paraneoplastic retinopathy
Confusing AZOOR with retinitis pigmentosa given overlapping photoreceptor dysfunction
Over-treating stable disease with immunosuppression of unproven benefit
management: Recognise that no established disease-modifying therapy exists and observe stable, non-progressive disease with serial monitoring
Consider a trial of systemic corticosteroid or steroid-sparing immunosuppression in progressive disease where an inflammatory mechanism is favoured
Monitor progression with fundus autofluorescence, spectral-domain optical coherence tomography, electroretinography and automated visual fields
Investigate for and exclude mimics, including paraneoplastic retinopathy with antiretinal antibodies and infective or inflammatory causes
Provide low-vision aids and rehabilitation for persistent scotomata and field loss
Refer to a medical retina or uveitis specialist and escalate treatment when zones expand or vision deteriorates
